title: How Good Are Frontier Models at Physics? Expert Re-Grading Reveals Broken Evaluations and Near-Saturation of Leading Benchmarks
authors: Ali Ansari, Haoran Sun, Andy Zeyi Liu, Mark Jabbour (core team), twelve physics advisors (Steven Girvin, A. Douglas Stone, David Poland and others), 32 further data auditors (39 auditors in all, some of them also advisors or core team), and the project advisors Lucas Baker, Arman Cohan and John Sous: 51 authors in all
lab: Yale University (most auditors), Jump Trading Group, University of Cambridge, University of Southern California; supported by Yale's Office of the Provost AI Initiatives and a gift from Jump Trading Group (correspondence: John Sous, Yale)
date: submitted 11 September 2026, announced 14 September 2026 (arXiv v1, the only version so far)

code.title: none released
code.link_label: no corrected questions or audit labels either
code.note: The paper releases neither its evaluation code nor the corrected and repaired question sets nor the per-question audit labels; the counts in its appendix are all there is. CritPt's official reference solutions are not public either, which is why the auditors re-derived them

takeaway: Domain experts re-graded six popular physics benchmarks and found wrong answer keys, ambiguous questions and grader bugs behind most reported model failures; corrected, frontier models look near-saturated, and the authors argue the next bar has to be harder human-written exams rather than another leaderboard on a broken quiz.
verdict: Believe the direction: of 250 rejected answers that physicists re-checked, 238 were the benchmark's or the grader's fault, and the defect rates (13% to 60% of items) are far above any frontier model's error rate. Treat the corrected percentages as upper estimates: only answers marked wrong were audited, the questions removed were picked by one model's failures, nothing marked right was ever checked, and no code or corrected questions are released.
